                                    PUC PROJECT No. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE                      § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION                               § TEXAS
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                       §

                                           Thor Equities


            Thor Equities’ Comments on PUCT Staff’s Proposal for Publication


I.    Introduction
Thor Equities submits these comments in response to PUCT Staff’s Proposal for Publication in the
above-captioned project to implement PURA § 37.0561. Thor Equities is an investment firm
actively developing large-scale power infrastructure projects in Texas and has a direct and
substantial interest in the rules governing large load interconnection.
Thor Equities recognizes the need to reduce the number of unqualified or speculative applications
to ensure limited resources are applied appropriately. Thor Equities respectfully urges the
Commission to address the concerns identified below prior to approving PUCT Staff’s Proposal
for Publication.
We are deeply concerned that, if the proposed rules are applied beyond Batch Zero to ongoing
batch processes, they risk effectively significantly diminishing Texas as a viable on-grid data
center market. The financial security requirements proposed coupled with the non-refundability of
such requirements are excessive and few data center operators will take such a large speculative
gamble.

Texas has a substantial community of landowners, developers, and investors who have committed
meaningful time and capital to site preparation in anticipation of data center development. If the
proposed financial commitment structure is extended to future batch processes without
modification, a significant portion of those projects are likely to become economically unviable.
The Commission should be aware that this outcome would generate considerable opposition from
a broad and influential group of Texas stakeholders. We urge the Commission to consider
modifications that would allow developers to obtain at least preliminary study feedback before
requiring material financial commitments, so that the process encourages rather than deters
responsible investment in Texas.


II.   Areas of common concern with other developers
Thor Equities has significant comments and concerns regarding the proposed rule’s treatment of
site control obligations, financial security timing and structure, non-refundable fees, and long-lead-
time equipment ownership. Each concern is addressed below with a full statement of the issue and
Thor Equities’ proposed remedy.
 a.   Proposed Subsection (d)(1): Site Control Requirements
       Issue: Proposed Subsection (d)(1) requires a large load customer to have executed a lease
or purchased land outright or an option to purchase or lease for its proposed project site at the
Intermediate Agreement phase before any interconnection study has been initiated.


       Comment: A developer has no basis on which to commit to a specific site location through
only a binding lease or purchase before receiving any visibility into whether that site can be
interconnected, at what capacity, and at what cost. Thor Equities wishes to emphasize that ensuring
acceptance of site control instruments at the Intermediate Agreement phase, including Purchase
and Sale Agreements, or Options to Purchase, is therefore paramount. These instruments provide
meaningful evidence of site commitment while preserving the developer’s ability to adapt to the
findings of the interconnection study.


b. Proposed Subsections (d)(10) and (d)(11): Excessive Financial Security at the
Intermediate Agreement Phase
        Issue: The proposed rule requires large load customers to post per-MW financial security
at the Intermediate Agreement phase, before any interconnection study has been conducted. At
this point, the developer has no confirmed interconnection path, no approved capacity, and no
validated basis on which to size its project. Requiring significant per-MW financial security
against an unvalidated capacity request exposes developers to substantial financial risk on projects
that may need to be redesigned, reduced in scope, or relocated following study findings. This
timing discourages good-faith participation and creates a structural competitive disadvantage
relative to better-capitalized incumbents.


The $50,000 per MW intermediate agreement financial security contemplated under the proposed
PGRR/NPRR framework would impose a financial security obligation of $50 million on a 1 GW
project. This figure far exceeds what is necessary to screen out speculative applications and will
impose a prohibitive barrier on the very class of large load customers—hyperscale data centers,
advanced manufacturing facilities, and large industrial users—that the rule is intended to attract
and accommodate.


Proposed Remedy: Any financial security posted at this stage should be fully refundable upon
withdrawal of the interconnection request, net only of amounts actually owed for costs already
incurred.


Thor Equities acknowledges that some level of upfront financial commitment is appropriate to
deter speculative queue positions and to ensure that only applicants with genuine project intent
advance through the interconnection process. However, the financial security must be calibrated
to serve that screening function without simultaneously deterring substantive investment. A
financial security of $50,000 per MW does not serve a screening purpose proportionate to its
 burden; it simply concentrates queue access to an extremely short list of firms, who have the
deepest access to capital. Texas has a compelling interest in attracting large load investment to
support economic growth, job creation, and grid revenue. A financial security structure that deters
that investment is contrary to the Commission’s statutory objectives and to the state’s broader
economic policy goals.
        Thor Equities proposes the following restructured approach:
      • A per-MW refundable financial security of $10,000 per MW, payable before the
         interconnection study begins. This amount is sufficient to demonstrate genuine project
         intent, without imposing a financial burden that is disproportionate to the stage of the
         process. For a 1 GW project, this equates to a $10 million security—a meaningful
         commitment that screens out speculative filers while remaining accessible to serious
         developers.
      • A fixed study fee of $300,000 for applications involving requested peak demand in
         excess of 150 MW, payable at application submission to fund the cost of the
         interconnection study itself. This fee should be independent of the per-MW financial
         security and should not be credited against any subsequent financial security obligation.
         Any additional costs in excess to be paid by the requestor subject to a pre-agreed cap at
         the outset of the study. It is important that costs are bounded to limit commercial risk and
         increase certainty at this stage of early project development.
      • Any per-MW financial security posted prior to the study should be fully refundable if the
         study results demonstrate that the requested capacity cannot be interconnected at the
         proposed site at a cost and timescale that the developer assesses as commercially
         reasonable, providing a meaningful off-ramp for applicants whose projects are rendered
         unviable by study findings through no fault of their own.

c.   Proposed Subsection (f)(7): Non-Refundable $50,000/MW Interconnection Fee
Issue: Proposed Subsection (f)(7) imposes a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per
MW of contracted peak demand at the Interconnection Agreement phase. This fee is unjustified.
Large load customers are already required to fund 100% of their direct interconnection costs
through contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) and to post financial security for long-lead-
time equipment and transmission upgrades. A non refundable per-MW fee untethered to any
specific cost incurred on the customer’s behalf violates the Commission’s cost-causation
principles. The mechanism of applying this fee as an offset to a TDSP’s rate base also risks over-
collection of revenue and introduces unnecessary complexity into the ratemaking process.
Proposed Remedy: The $50,000 per MW non-refundable interconnection fee in Subsection (f)(7)
should be eliminated. There should be two options: 1) A minimum demand charge embedded in
the TDSP’s tariff—tied to actual cost recovery—would be a more appropriate, transparent, and
legally defensible mechanism to allow a regulated rate of return or 2) A large load customer
provides the capital with a refundable fee for the transmission and other upgrades (costs of
infrastructure upgrades incurred would be deducted) but there is no minimum demand charge. This
is because a large load customer may be able to have access to capital at a lower rate than a
regulated TSP and may not want to be obligated for long term minimum demand charges. Thor
Equities would propose the large load should pay a minimum transmission charge for five years
following energization, with a minimum billing demand of no less than 50 percent of the
 customer's contracted peak demand. This has been endorsed by major hyperscalers in recent
projects.


d. Proposed Subsections (g)(3)/(g)(4) and (h)(3)/(h)(4): Unfair 80/20 Refund Split on
Withdrawal and Underutilization
Issue: The proposed rule imposes an 80/20 split on residual financial security balances when a
large load customer withdraws its interconnection request or fails to meet a milestone in its
energization schedule. Under this structure, the interconnecting TDSP retains 80% of any unspent
balance remaining after all outstanding amounts owed have been satisfied, with only 20% returned
to the customer. This outcome is not grounded in cost-causation principles. Once a TDSP has
recovered all costs actually incurred on the customer’s behalf, there is no legitimate basis for
retaining the remaining balance. The TDSP has been made whole; retaining 80% of the surplus
constitutes a windfall. Furthermore, permitting TDSPs to treat residual financial security as a
revenue stream creates perverse incentives and is incompatible with the Commission’s regulatory
obligations.


If the results are unfavorable and the developer withdraws, only 20% of the financial security is
refundable, meaning the effective cost of simply obtaining a study could in the case of a 1 GW
study would be $40 million dollars with no guarantee of a viable interconnection path.
Few organizations will accept this level of financial risk under conditions of such uncertainty. The
likely result is that data center developers will redirect capital to other states with more accessible
interconnection processes or will pursue fully behind-the-meter campus configurations that
remove them from the grid entirely.

Either outcome represents a significant loss for Texas. The state would forgo billions of dollars in
investment, tax revenue, and economic activity that large-scale data centers generate. Equally
important, it would lose the meaningful grid benefits that on-grid data centers can provide —
including load flexibility, support for renewable integration, and reduced per-unit infrastructure
costs spread across a broader customer base.


Proposed Remedy: The Commission should require TDSPs to refund 100% of unspent financial
security balances after all outstanding amounts owed have been satisfied. Residual financial
security is the customer’s property and must be returned in full. The Commission should reject
any mechanism that allows TSPs to profit from the departure or underperformance of large load
customers.


e. Long-Lead-Time Equipment Funded by Large Load Customers: Redeployment
Rights
Issue: The proposed rule does not adequately address ownership and deployment rights of long-
lead-time equipment that has been fully funded by a large load customer. Under the current
proposal, a customer who has paid in full for such equipment and enabled the purchase —such as
 transformers or other critical grid components—may be denied title to that equipment and the
ability to redeploy it at an alternative site. This is commercially unjust and creates a significant
disincentive to early procurement of materials with long manufacturing and delivery timelines,
precisely the activity the rule should be encouraging. Thor Equities understands that the financial
security posted ensures that the TDSP is covered for any expense incurred, if the project is halted
or cancelled.
Proposed Remedy: Where a large load customer has fully funded long-lead-time equipment, the
proposed rule should be amended to provide preferential redeployment rights for that equipment
with the large load customer rather than in the interconnecting TDSP. The customer should retain
the unconditional right to redeploy that equipment at an alternative site within the same TDSP, if
its original interconnection request is withdrawn or modified. The large load customer would need
to provide written notification within 30 days of cancelling on their intention for redeployment to
a specific named project that had already been submitted. This option can be limited to 36 months
to ensure that the large load customer is not preventing use by other customers in the queue. TDSP
would have right to charge large load customers for any additional costs related to storage.

III.   Additional Concerns Specific to Thor Equities


a. Regulatory Communication and Transition Protections
Large load interconnection projects involve capital commitments and construction timelines
measured in years. Regulatory changes to interconnection rules, particularly those affecting
transient behavior, ramp rate constraints, and energization milestones, can materially affect project
economics after a developer has made irreversible financial commitments. The proposed rule
contains no provision requiring advance notice of such changes or protecting applicants who have
already executed agreements from retroactive application of new requirements.
        Thor Equities proposes the following protections:
      • A minimum twelve (12)-month advance written notice period before any new regulation
          or material modification affecting transient behavior, ramp rate constraints, or
          interconnection procedures becomes effective for applicants already in the queue.
      • Grandfathering protection for applicants who have executed an Intermediate Agreement
          or Interconnection Agreement prior to the effective date of any new rule, ensuring their
          obligations and rights are governed by the rules in effect at the time of execution.


IV.    Conclusion
Thor Equities respectfully urges the Commission to address the concerns identified in these
comments before approving PUCT Staff’s Proposal for Publication. Thor Equities’ proposed
modifications are grounded in cost-causation principles, commercial practicality, and the
Commission’s stated objective of facilitating large load interconnection in a manner that is fair,
predictable, and conducive to long-term investment in Texas’s grid infrastructure.
Thor Equities remains available to provide additional information or technical analysis at the
Commission’s request.
 Executive Summary
1. Financial security must be proportionate and study informed
Proposed Subsections (d)(10) and (d)(11)
Issue: A $50,000/MW pre-study financial security requires a 1 GW applicant to commit $50
million before a single study has been conducted, with no confirmed interconnection path. This
will deter legitimate data center investment and restrict queue access to a narrow group of the most
capitalised incumbents — contrary to Texas's economic development interests.
Proposal: Replace the pre-study deposit with a $10,000/MW refundable security plus a fixed
$300,000 study fee for applications above 150 MW. The per-MW security should be fully
refundable if the study demonstrates the site is not commercially viable to connect

2. The non refundable interconnection fee should be replaced with a tariff mechanism
Proposed Subsection (f)(7)
Issue: A non-refundable $50,000/MW fee at the Interconnection Agreement phase is duplicative
as developers already fund direct grid costs through CIAC. The fee is untethered to any specific
cost incurred on the customer's behalf and violates cost-causation principles.
Proposal: Eliminate the non-refundable per-MW fee. Replace it with a minimum demand charge
in the TDSP's tariff, set at no less than 50% of contracted peak demand for five years following
energization. This approach, already endorsed by major hyperscalers, ensures ongoing cost
recovery, and protects existing ratepayers through a transparent, legally defensible mechanism.

3. Withdrawing developers should receive full refund of unspent financial security
Proposed Subsections (g)(3)/(g)(4) and (h)(3)/(h)(4)
Issue: The 80/20 split allows the TDSP to retain 80% of any unspent financial security balance
after a withdrawal, even after recovering all actual costs incurred. For a 1 GW applicant, the
effective cost of obtaining a study that yields an unviable result could reach $40 million — a level
of unrecoverable risk that will drive data center developers to other states or to fully off-grid
configurations, depriving Texas of investment, tax revenue, and grid benefits.
Proposal: Require TDSPs to refund 100% of unspent financial security after all actual costs have
been recovered. Residual security is the customer's property. Allowing TDSPs to profit from
developer withdrawals creates perverse incentives incompatible with the Commission's cost-
causation obligations.

4. Customers who fund long lead equipment should retain redeployment rights Section II(f)
Issue: Developers who fully fund long-lead-time equipment, such as high-voltage transformers,
may be denied the right to redeploy that equipment if their original interconnection request is
withdrawn, despite having funded and enabled the entire procurement cost
Proposal: Where a customer has fully funded long-lead-time equipment, the rule should vest
preferential redeployment rights for that customer to another project in the same TDSP territory,.
The customer should have the right to redeploy equipment to another named project within the
same TDSP territory, exercisable within 36 months upon 30 days' written notice. The TDSP may
charge for reasonable storage costs during this period.
 Respectfully submitted,




______________________________


Faraz Ahmad
Head of Energy & Infrastructure
Thor Equities
